summary.headline: A rate-driven bond dealer still losing money, priced near 1.8x a shrinking book
summary.text:
Capital Alliance PLC (CALT.N0000) is a government-securities primary dealer, 86% owned by Capital Alliance Holdings. It funds a book of Treasury bills and bonds mainly with repos, so it earns a thin interest spread (1.47% in 2025/26) and, much more, trading gains when interest rates fall and losses when they rise. The rate cuts of 2022–2024 gave profits of Rs 2.83bn, Rs 13.89bn and Rs 4.42bn; in the calmer 2025/26 profit was Rs 2.00bn (EPS Rs 6.07, ROE 15.7%). In the six months to September 2026 yields moved against it and it lost Rs 3.51bn (EPS −Rs 10.66), most of it in the first quarter (about −Rs 2.81bn, calculated; Q2 −Rs 0.70bn). After Rs 16.00 a share of dividends for 2025/26 (263% of profit) and the loss, NAV fell from Rs 43.70 (March 2025) to Rs 33.76 and then Rs 23.11 (September 2026). It has since cut the bond book from Rs 81.1bn to Rs 34.6bn and sold all its quoted shares.

At Rs 42.30 (CSE close, 25 November 2026) the share is 1.8x NAV, which needs a long-run ROE of about 28% at the 18.3% cost of equity: close to the 2024/25 rate-cut year, not a normal one. Four book- and earnings-based methods, all calculated by code, with a through-the-cycle ROE of 20% in the base case, give a fair value of about Rs 23.50 (was Rs 25.70: the cost of equity now comes from the house formula, the P/E multiples were cut to the justified levels, and the dividend and residual income methods now assume a three-year recovery from the current losses). The price is about 80% above it: overpriced. Buy at up to Rs 20.00; under Rs 17.64 is a strong buy (about 0.75–0.85x NAV). It still passes three of the four business tests (high returns over several years, capital well above the minimum, cash dividends) and fails on steady profit, so it stays on the watch list (category 2). The upside case is a fall in yields, which would bring trading gains back quickly.

models.comment: Rs 0 / 1.00 / 3.00 next year, growing 5% / 6% / 7% (within the supported 4.4% / 7.3% / 11.0%) for three years; then normalised EPS with the stable payout 1 − g ÷ ROE (58% / 70% / 77%), at the cost of equity.

models.name: Residual income
models.comment: Book Rs 23.11; ROE moves from −30.3% (last twelve months, calculated) to 12% / 20% / 30% over three years, 63% payout, then excess returns grow at 5% / 6% / 7%. The lowest method because it charges for the losses still being made.

modelsNote: Four methods, all calculated by scripts/valuation.py from modelInputs. Growth check: supported growth is 0% on 2025/26 alone (payout 263%) and 4.4% / 7.3% / 11.0% through the cycle (36.5% of profit kept over 2022/23–2025/26 × long-run ROE); long-run growth of 5% / 6% / 7% is within 2 points in every case. The long-run ROE is the key choice: 20% in the base case, between the two calmer years (15.7% and 28.7%). Ratio check (docs/ratio-ranges.md): beta 0.98 and cost of equity 18.3% are in range; long-run growth is below the 12.24% bond yield; the bull ROE of 30% and leverage of 4–6x are outside the normal ranges, which is the nature of a primary dealer. fullText:
Capital Alliance PLC (CALT.N0000) is a government-securities primary dealer, 86% owned by Capital Alliance Holdings. It funds a book of Treasury bills and bonds mainly with repos, so it earns a thin interest spread (1.47% in 2025/26) and, much more, trading gains when interest rates fall and losses when they rise. The rate cuts of 2022–2024 gave profits of Rs 2.83bn, Rs 13.89bn and Rs 4.42bn; in the calmer 2025/26 profit was Rs 2.00bn (EPS Rs 6.07, ROE 15.7%). In the six months to September 2026 yields moved against it and it lost Rs 3.51bn (EPS −Rs 10.66), most of it in the first quarter (about −Rs 2.81bn, calculated; Q2 −Rs 0.70bn). After Rs 16.00 a share of dividends for 2025/26 (263% of profit) and the loss, NAV fell from Rs 43.70 (March 2025) to Rs 33.76 and then Rs 23.11 (September 2026). It has since cut the bond book from Rs 81.1bn to Rs 34.6bn and sold all its quoted shares.

At Rs 42.30 (CSE close, 25 November 2026) the share is 1.8x NAV, which needs a long-run ROE of about 28% at the 18.3% cost of equity: close to the 2024/25 rate-cut year, not a normal one. Four book- and earnings-based methods, all calculated by code, with a through-the-cycle ROE of 20% in the base case, give a fair value of about Rs 23.50 (was Rs 25.70: the cost of equity now comes from the house formula, the P/E multiples were cut to the justified levels, and the dividend and residual income methods now assume a three-year recovery from the current losses). The price is about 80% above it: overpriced. Buy at up to Rs 20.00; under Rs 17.64 is a strong buy (about 0.75–0.85x NAV). It still passes three of the four business tests (high returns over several years, capital well above the minimum, cash dividends) and fails on steady profit, so it stays on the watch list (category 2). The upside case is a fall in yields, which would bring trading gains back quickly.

Valuation table (Rs per share)
Method | Bear | Base | Bull | Weighted
Justified price to book | 10.93 | 26.30 | 54.24 | 27.28
P/E on normalised earnings | 10.81 | 25.42 | 52.00 | 26.35
Dividend model | 7.36 | 21.20 | 48.78 | 22.56
Residual income | 4.97 | 16.75 | 40.20 | 17.91
Average | 8.52 | 22.42 | 48.81 | 23.52

How the business makes money: CAL buys Treasury bills and bonds and funds most of them with repos. In a normal year the spread between the two (1.47% in 2025/26) gives net interest income of about Rs 2.5–3.0bn. The big swings come from trading and remeasurement: Rs 19.0bn of trading gains in 2023/24 when rates were cut sharply, Rs 6.1bn in 2024/25, Rs 3.0bn in 2025/26 (less Rs 1.8bn of remeasurement losses), and a Rs 3.82bn loss in the six months to September 2026. A 1-point rise in rates would have cut pre-tax profit by about Rs 0.85bn on the March 2026 book (Rs 2.42bn a year earlier, when the bond book was bigger).

What happened in 2026/27 so far: net interest income fell to Rs 0.56bn (Rs 1.38bn a year earlier) and losses on financial assets were Rs 3.82bn (trading −Rs 3.53bn, of which government securities −Rs 3.65bn; remeasurement −Rs 0.29bn). The interim report gives no commentary; the losses point to rising yields. Q2 (−Rs 0.70bn) was much smaller than Q1 (about −Rs 2.81bn, calculated), but Q2 net interest income was only Rs 0.23bn. Almost no tax was charged on the loss. The bond book was cut from Rs 81.1bn to Rs 34.6bn, repos and bank loans from Rs 72.2bn to Rs 33.0bn, and all quoted shares (Rs 0.89bn) were sold.

Required return: cost of equity 18.3% from the house formula (risk-free 8.24% + beta 0.98 × 10.28% equity premium including the country premium), bear 19.8%, bull 16.8%. The beta is Damodaran's global brokerage and investment banking figure, the same as for First Capital; it is provisional until the January 2027 refresh. No WACC: a dealer's borrowing is its raw material, so it is valued on equity.

Why the price looks high: at 18.3% Rs 42.30 needs a long-run ROE of about 28% on today's book. CAL earned that only in the rate-cut years; its 'normal' year 2025/26 gave 15.7% and the last 12 months −30%. A base ROE of 20% is already generous. Growth check: the company kept about 36.5% of its profit over 2022/23–2025/26, which at a 20% ROE supports about 7% growth; the 5% / 6% / 7% long-run growth used is within that.

What changed from the 13 November analysis: the cost of equity now comes from the house formula (18.3% base, was 18.5% set by hand); the P/E multiples were cut from 5x / 6x / 8x to 3.9x / 5.5x / 7.5x so none is above the justified P/E; the dividend model now assumes three lean years (Rs 0 / 1.00 / 3.00) before the stable payout, and the residual income model starts from the actual last-twelve-month ROE (−30%) rather than a hand-set first year. All four methods are now calculated by code. Fair value Rs 25.70 → Rs 23.52; buy Rs 21.80 → Rs 20.00; strong buy Rs 19.30 → Rs 17.64.

Dividends: Rs 19.50 for 2024/25 and Rs 16.00 for 2025/26 (Rs 4.00 + Rs 12.00 interims), far above profits, which is why book value has halved. Policy is to pay at most 50% of the year's profit (CBSL rules for primary dealers), so I assume nothing for 2026/27; the base case has Rs 1.00 in the next twelve months. The 38% 'yield' on last year's dividend won't be repeated.

Capital: core capital Rs 11.01bn and capital ratio 20.84% in March 2026, against minimums of Rs 4.0bn (Rs 5.0bn from 1 January 2027) and 10%. Equity has since fallen to Rs 7.61bn; another loss like Q1 would bring it close to Rs 5bn and could force a smaller book or new capital.

Management and plans: the five-year plan is to become a full fixed income house (derivatives, a corporate bond market, CAL Portal and TradeX for retail investors) and to earn more from fees so that profit depends less on rate calls. The first half of 2026/27 shows no sign of that yet: it was a rate-driven loss. The board also changed: Mr W A T Fernando, the founder and former CEO, is listed as Chairman at 30 September 2026 in place of Mr D A De Zoysa.

Shareholders: Capital Alliance Holdings PLC holds 86.00%; the public 12.41% (8,862 holders, up from 8,710 in March). Nothing moved among the large holders in the six months.

Buy plan: 200 shares up to Rs 23.50, 150 up to Rs 20.00 and 150 up to Rs 17.60, about Rs 10,340 in total (average Rs 20.68), against Rs 21,150 at Rs 42.30. The lowest prices of the last two years were Rs 39.80 (2024/25) and Rs 42.80 (July–September 2026), so the plan needs further losses or a market fall; don't chase it.

Business tests: 3 of 4 passed (fails steady profit), so it's rated good, but the price is far above the buy price: watch list (category 2), unchanged.

Uncertain: EPS, NAV per share and dividends per share before 2024/25 aren't in these reports. The September 2026 capital ratio and the split of repos and bank loans aren't given. The beta is a global sector figure, not a local one.
